related_questions.snippet: Call 911 or emergency medical services if your blood pressure is 180/120 mm Hg or greater and you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or symptoms of stroke. Stroke symptoms include: Numbness or tingling. Loss of feeling in the face, arm or leg, often on just one side of the body.

related_questions.question: What is considered stroke level for high blood pressure?

text_blocks.snippet: A blood pressure reading of 180/120 mmHg or higher is considered a hypertensive crisis, a medical emergency that can lead to a stroke. This level of high blood pressure requires immediate medical attention.
Understanding the Numbers

list.snippet: Systolic Pressure (top number): Measures the force of blood against artery walls when the heart beats.
Diastolic Pressure (bottom number): Measures the force of blood against artery walls between heartbeats.
180/120 mmHg or higher: Indicates a hypertensive crisis, a potentially life-threatening situation.

text_blocks.snippet: Why is it dangerous?

Extremely high blood pressure can damage blood vessels, especially in the brain, increasing the risk of stroke. A hypertensive crisis can also lead to other serious health problems, including heart attack.
What to do if your blood pressure is 180/120 or higher:

list.snippet: Seek immediate medical help: Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.
Don't delay: Prompt treatment is crucial to minimize potential damage.

Be aware of other symptoms: Chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, vision changes, difficulty speaking, confusion, dizziness, or vomiting can also indicate a hypertensive crisis.

related_questions.question: Should I go to the hospital if my blood pressure is 140 over 90?

text_blocks.snippet: A blood pressure reading of 140/90 mmHg, while considered Stage 2 hypertension, doesn't automatically necessitate a trip to the hospital. It's advisable to monitor the reading and consult with a healthcare professional for personalized guidance. If the reading is consistently high (over several readings) or accompanied by symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, vision changes, or stroke-like symptoms, then immediate medical attention is crucial, according to the Mayo Clinic.
snippet_highlighted_words: doesn't automatically necessitate a trip to the hospital

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed breakdown:
Understanding Blood Pressure Readings:

list.snippet: Normal: 120/80 mmHg or lower.
Elevated: 120-129/80 mmHg.
Stage 1 Hypertension: 130-139/80-89 mmHg.
Stage 2 Hypertension: 140/90 mmHg or higher.
Hypertensive Crisis: 180/120 mmHg or higher.

text_blocks.snippet: When to Seek Immediate Medical Care:

list.title: Hypertensive Crisis:
list.snippet: If your blood pressure reaches 180/120 mmHg or higher, and you experience symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, vision changes, or stroke-like symptoms (weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking), it's crucial to call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room immediately, says www.heart.org.

list.title: Severe Symptoms:
list.snippet: Even without a hypertensive crisis reading, if you experience chest pain, severe headache, shortness of breath, or other concerning symptoms, seek immediate medical attention.

list.title: Repeated High Readings:
list.snippet: If you consistently get readings of 140/90 mmHg or higher over multiple readings and are concerned, consult your doctor promptly, according to GoodRx.

text_blocks.snippet: When to See Your Doctor Soon:

list.snippet: If your blood pressure is consistently in the Stage 2 hypertension range (140/90 mmHg or higher), even without symptoms, schedule an appointment with your doctor to discuss management and treatment options.
Your doctor can assess your overall health, determine the cause of your high blood pressure, and recommend appropriate lifestyle changes and/or medications.

text_blocks.snippet: What to Do in the Meantime:

list.title: Relax and Recheck:
list.snippet: If you're not experiencing any symptoms, try relaxing for a few minutes and recheck your blood pressure. Sometimes, a high reading can be due to stress or anxiety.

list.title: Monitor Your Blood Pressure:
list.snippet: Keep a record of your blood pressure readings, including the date and time, to share with your doctor.

list.title: Follow Your Doctor's Advice:
list.snippet: If you're already taking medication for high blood pressure, continue to follow your doctor's instructions.

related_questions.question: What BP warrants an ER visit?

text_blocks.snippet: A hypertensive crisis, with a blood pressure reading of 180/120 mm Hg or higher, requires immediate medical attention, potentially in an emergency room. If accompanied by symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, or vision changes, it's crucial to call 911 immediately. Even without noticeable symptoms, blood pressure this high warrants prompt medical evaluation.
Here's a more detailed breakdown:
When to go to the ER for high blood pressure:

list.title: Hypertensive Crisis (180/120 or higher):
list.snippet: This is a serious condition that can lead to organ damage if not treated promptly.

list.title: With Symptoms:
list.snippet: If you experience any of the following symptoms along with a blood pressure reading of 180/120 or higher, go to the ER immediately or call 911: chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, vision changes, numbness or weakness, difficulty speaking, seizures, chest pain, or breathing difficulty.

list.title: Without Symptoms:
list.snippet: Even without noticeable symptoms, a blood pressure of 180/120 or higher requires prompt medical attention. It could be a hypertensive emergency or urgency, and a doctor needs to assess the situation.

list.title: Hypertensive Urgency (180/120 or higher without symptoms):
list.snippet: This is a high blood pressure reading without organ damage symptoms. While not immediately life-threatening, it requires prompt medical attention and possible medication adjustments.

list.title: Hypertensive Emergency (180/120 or higher with symptoms):
list.snippet: This is a medical emergency that requires immediate treatment, often in an ER.

text_blocks.snippet: Important Considerations:

list.title: Recheck if No Symptoms:
list.snippet: If your blood pressure is 180/120 or higher but you have no symptoms, recheck it after a few minutes of rest. If it remains high, seek medical advice.

list.title: Consult Your Doctor:
list.snippet: If you're unsure about your blood pressure readings or whether you need to go to the ER, contact your doctor for guidance.

text_blocks.snippet: A blood pressure reading of 180/120 mmHg or higher, especially when accompanied by symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, or vision changes, indicates a hypertensive emergency and requires immediate medical attention. This situation can cause serious, even life-threatening, damage to organs like the heart, brain, and kidneys if not addressed promptly.
What is a Hypertensive Emergency?

A hypertensive emergency is a severe and sudden increase in blood pressure that can lead to organ damage. It's characterized by a blood pressure reading of 180/120 mmHg or higher, and often includes symptoms like:

list.snippet: Chest pain: A sign of potential heart problems.
Shortness of breath: May indicate lung or heart issues.
Severe headache: A common symptom of dangerously high blood pressure.
Vision changes: Blurred vision, double vision, or loss of vision can occur.
Numbness or weakness: May suggest a stroke or other neurological issues.
Difficulty speaking: Another sign of potential stroke or neurological damage.
Back pain: Can be a sign of aortic dissection, a serious condition.
Loss of consciousness: A critical sign of severe hypertension and potential brain damage.

text_blocks.snippet: When to Seek Emergency Care:
If you experience a blood pressure reading of 180/120 mmHg or higher, especially with any of the above symptoms, seek immediate medical attention. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.
What Happens During a Hypertensive Emergency?

In a hypertensive emergency, blood pressure is so high that it can cause damage to vital organs. The goal of treatment is to lower blood pressure gradually to prevent further damage. This often involves administering medication intravenously in a hospital setting.
Important Considerations:

list.title: Individual differences:
list.snippet: What constitutes a hypertensive emergency can vary slightly from person to person, especially for those with pre-existing conditions.

list.title: Symptoms are crucial:
list.snippet: Even if your blood pressure is not as high as 180/120 mmHg, if you experience any symptoms of a hypertensive crisis, seek medical care immediately.

list.title: Prevention is key:
list.snippet: Regular blood pressure monitoring and management are crucial for preventing hypertensive crises.
